hints: Start by thinking about what xylem sap and phloem sap actually carry - mineral ions one way, sugars like sucrose the other way. What must the main liquid be able to do with those solutes?
Now link water structure to movement - how do hydrogen bonds between water molecules, and between water and walls, help pull sap up, and how does adding water build pressure to push sap along?
walkthrough:
Why So Much Water - Dissolving Things**
Think of sap as a delivery solution. Xylem carries mineral ions and phloem carries sucrose and amino acids. Because water is polar, it is an excellent solvent, so these solutes dissolve easily and can be carried in solution in large volumes.

Why Water Itself Helps It Move**
Water also has the right physical properties for the transport mechanism. In xylem, hydrogen bonding gives cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to cellulose in the xylem wall, so a continuous transpiration stream can be pulled up. In phloem, movement of water by osmosis builds up hydrostatic pressure, creating the pressure gradient that drives mass flow from source to sink.

Final answer: Water is a good solvent so ions / minerals / assimilates dissolve in it for transport in xylem and phloem sap; cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to xylem walls supports the transpiration stream and water builds hydrostatic pressure gradient for mass flow / translocation in phloem.

hints: Follow sucrose from its birthplace. It is made in photosynthesising leaf cells, then has to get to the conducting tube. Which route uses living cytoplasmic connections?
Loading sucrose against a concentration gradient needs energy. Which neighbouring cell is packed with mitochondria and membrane pumps to create a hydrogen ion gradient?
Remember which phloem cell has no nucleus, few organelles and depends on its neighbour for metabolic support, and simply receives sucrose to carry it away.
walkthrough:
Event A - Moving Through Plasmodesmata**
Sucrose made in the mesophyll moves by diffusion through plasmodesmata toward the phloem. The cell that receives it through plasmodesmata from the companion cell is the conducting cell itself, the phloem sieve tube element. It is highly modified with no nucleus and sieve plates to allow bulk flow.

Event B - Pumping Hydrogen Ions Out**
To load sucrose actively, a proton gradient is needed. The companion cell uses ATP from its many mitochondria to pump hydrogen ions out through proton pumps in its membrane. This creates an electrochemical gradient with more $H^+$ outside than inside.

Event C - Cotransporting Sucrose In**
Hydrogen ions then flow back down their gradient through sucrose-$H^+$ cotransporter proteins, dragging sucrose with them into the same cell. That cell is again the companion cell. From there sucrose passes through plasmodesmata into the adjacent sieve tube element for translocation.
Final answer: A - phloem sieve tube element; B - companion cell; C - companion cell.
